1.description:
Eck Robertson recorded 'Sallie Gooden' for Victor in New York on July 1, 1922. His solo recording is an early example of Texas-style variations on a short fiddle melody. The Discography of American Historical Recordings lists Robertson as the arranger, not the composer.

Henry Reed also recorded the tune for the Library of Congress in 1966. These are separate versions, not credits for every recording on this page.

Sources: UC Santa Barbara, Discography of American Historical Recordings, Victor matrix B-26664; American Folklife Center, Library of Congress.
1.notes: Robertson's 1922 recording offers one approach to building variations around the base melody.

2.description: 'Fire on the Mountain' has been recorded by Bill Monroe, Flatt and Scruggs, and Tommy Jarrell. Versions differ, so these names describe part of the tune's recording history rather than the performer of every recording linked here.

3.description:
'Old Joe Clark' circulated as both a song and a fiddle tune, with many comic verses. The Traditional Tune Archive discusses its use as a play-party tune and notes Alan Jabbour's observation that he had found no nineteenth-century printed examples. That is not evidence that the melody was composed in the twentieth century.

Stories identifying Joe Clark with a particular Kentucky resident are not a secure origin for the tune. Ira Ford included it in Traditional Music in America (1940).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org), adapted from The Fiddler's Companion by Andrew Kuntz.
3.notes: Versions differ in their use of G natural and G sharp. Check the version being played before choosing accompaniment.

4.description: 'Shady Grove' is an Appalachian song with floating verses and several melodic settings. Jean Ritchie, Doc Watson, and Clarence Ashley helped bring it to folk-revival audiences. Their versions need not match the key or arrangement of the recording here.

5.description:
'Cripple Creek' circulated as a song and a fiddle tune before becoming part of the bluegrass repertoire. Ira Ford included it in Traditional Music in America (1940). Collections document versions in several keys and fiddle tunings.

The title has been linked to places in both Virginia and Colorado; it does not establish a single place of origin.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org).

7.description: 'Whiskey Before Breakfast' is played in old-time and Celtic sessions. Its origins are uncertain.

8.description:
'Arkansas Traveler' is associated with Sandford C. 'Sandy' Faulkner and a comic dialogue between a traveler and a fiddler. The familiar story describes the traveler completing the tune and winning the fiddler's hospitality; it is a story attached to the tune, not a documented account of its composition.

Henry Reed recorded a version for the Library of Congress in 1967.

Source: American Folklife Center, Library of Congress.

9.description:
'Soldier's Joy' appears in eighteenth-century collections and later became part of the American fiddle repertoire. Henry Reed recorded a version for the Library of Congress in 1967.

Source: American Folklife Center, Library of Congress.

10.description:
Alan and Karen Singer Jabbour recorded Henry Reed playing 'Kitchen Girl' at his home in Glen Lyn, Virginia, on June 18, 1966. The Hollow Rock String Band learned it from Reed, and its recording helped other fiddlers pick up the tune. The Library of Congress notes general resemblances to other melodies but no clear variant.

Source: Fiddle Tunes of the Old Frontier: The Henry Reed Collection, American Folklife Center, Library of Congress.

11.description:
'John Henry' tells of a Black steel-driver who competes against a steam drill. The story circulated in work songs and ballads before appearing in many instrumental versions. Guy Johnson examined the legend in his 1929 book John Henry: Tracking Down a Negro Legend.

The historical person and the location of the contest remain disputed; the tune does not settle those questions.

12.description:
'Angeline the Baker' is related to Stephen Foster's 1850 song 'Angelina Baker,' whose lyrics describe an enslaved woman separated from her lover by sale. An early fiddle version was recorded by Uncle Eck Dunford for Victor in 1928. The tune appears in David Brody's Fiddler's Fakebook (1982).

The recording here is by Tom Joad, preserved by the Internet Archive, not a recording of Foster or Dunford.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org).

13.description: 'Sandy River Belle' is associated with Tommy Jarrell and the Round Peak repertoire of North Carolina. His recorded version is one source for later players; it does not establish where the tune was composed or which river the title names.

14.description: The recording linked here is by Big Foot Lane, preserved by the Internet Archive. The tune's earlier history is not documented here.

17.description: 'Cluck Old Hen' is played both as an instrumental and with short, changing verses. Related titles can refer to different melodies, so a recording of 'Old Hen Cackled' should not automatically be treated as an early recording of this tune.

18.description:
'Bonaparte's Retreat' survives in several fiddle settings. Henry Reed recorded a version for the Library of Congress in 1966. The title recalls Napoleon, but it does not by itself establish the melody's age or route to America.

Source: American Folklife Center, Library of Congress.

19.description:
Henry Reed recorded 'Liberty' for the Library of Congress in 1966. This documents Reed's version, not the origin of all tunes that have used the title.

Source: American Folklife Center, Library of Congress.

151.description:
Seven Foot Dilly and His Dill Pickles recorded 'Bibb County Hoedown' in Atlanta in November 1930, with A. A. Gray on fiddle. The group belonged to the north Georgia string-band scene. The tune also appears in Gene Silberberg's Tunes I Learned at Tractor Tavern (2002).

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org).

156.description:
William 'Bill' Driver was born in Eldridge, Missouri, and spent much of his fiddling career in Miller County, near Iberia. His father, also William Driver, was born in 1859, adopted by the Driver family, and later worked as a Free Will Baptist circuit preacher. He died in 1934.

Driver's repertory is documented as part of the African American fiddle tradition of central Missouri.

Source: John Lamancusa collection, oldtimefiddletunes.net.

601.description:
'Railroad Runs Through Georgia' was in the repertory of the Collins family of Pottawatomie County, Oklahoma. Gary Stanton and Tom Carter made a field recording of Max Collins playing it. The tune is also associated with Marion Thede's Fiddle Book, page 42, in a setting notated by Walter Baker.

The documented setting uses AEae fiddle tuning.

Source: John Lamancusa collection, oldtimefiddletunes.net.

519.description:
Tater Joe's Old-Time Fiddle catalog lists 'Oak Ridge Stomp' among its D-tuning tunes. The listing does not name a composer or source fiddler.

Source: John Lamancusa collection, oldtimefiddletunes.net.

623.description:
Roger Sprung (1930–2023) was a banjo player and teacher whose repertoire extended beyond bluegrass to ragtime, jazz and other styles. He learned by ear from Earl Scruggs records and took lessons from Tom Paley. Those biographical details do not establish that he composed this tune.

Source: John Lamancusa collection, oldtimefiddletunes.net.

736.description:
Tom Fuller (1890–1979) grew up in Indian Territory, later Oklahoma, and worked in farming, ranching and oilfields in Oklahoma and west Texas. He bought his first fiddle around 1905 and learned by ear. In the early 1920s he took lessons in Hulen, Oklahoma, and learned to read music.

Source: John Lamancusa collection, oldtimefiddletunes.net.

767.description:
'Weller's Reel' is listed in the Traditional Tune Archive, which supplies notation but no composer or historical annotation. The listing is also reproduced at abcnotation.com.

Source: Traditional Tune Archive (tunearch.org).

921.description:
'Old Rusty Mill Waltz' is associated with Melvin Wine and his recording Hannah at the Springhouse. It also appears in John Lamancusa's Gettysburg Collection of Old-Time Fiddle Tunes. Wine's recording is a source for the tune, not proof that he composed it.

Source: John Lamancusa collection, oldtimefiddletunes.net.

973.description:
The Fiddler's Companion reports that Bob Holt thought he had learned 'Lonnie's Polka' from a radio broadcast by Missouri fiddler Lonnie Robertson. Holt was uncertain about the source and title, so this is a tentative account of transmission, not a composer credit.

Source: John Lamancusa collection, oldtimefiddletunes.net.

203.description:
'Cacklin Hen' and 'Cluck Old Hen' are easily confused titles, but they can refer to different tunes. Fiddlin' John Carson's 1923 'Old Hen Cackled and the Rooster's Going to Crow' should not be used to date this melody without comparing the versions.

Source: John Lamancusa collection, oldtimefiddletunes.net.
